theme: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 79. It is a communal lament written after the destruction of Jerusalem. Read it as the congregation’s cry after reading 2 Kings 25, and notice the way it moves from catastrophe to confession and to a request for forgiveness.
settingTheScene: Psalm 79 is a psalm of Asaph. It is one of the clearest psalms about the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, with the temple defiled, the city in ruins, and the bodies unburied. It pairs naturally with Jeremiah’s temple sermon, which warned this would happen. It is a prayer of those who know that part of the blame is their own.
observation: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins” (v. 1).
“They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food” (v. 2).
“We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us” (v. 4).
“How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever?” (v. 5).
“Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low” (v. 8).
“Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name” (v. 9).
“Why should the nations say, Where is their God?” (v. 10).
“But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with an inventory of ruin. The temple is defiled, the city is rubble, the dead are left unburied. The psalmist holds nothing back. The people have become a mockery to the neighbors, a taunt, and he asks the question every grieving believer asks: “How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever?”

But notice what the prayer does not do. It does not claim that Judah is innocent. “Do not remember against us our former iniquities.” The people know why this happened. The prophets had told them. The psalm joins confession with the cry for help. “Help us… deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name’s sake.” The word “atone” is the language of the temple, and it comes from a people who have lost their temple. They ask God himself to cover their sin.

The reason given for the appeal is God’s name. “Why should the nations say, Where is their God?” The people are not asking to be rescued because they deserve it, but because God’s reputation is bound up with theirs. This is the way of intercession in the Bible: to ask God to act for the sake of his own glory.

The psalm ends with a vow of praise. The people are “the sheep of your pasture.” The shepherd has allowed the wolves in, but the sheep still belong to him. They promise to give thanks forever and to tell the story from generation to generation. Even this psalm of ruin ends with testimony, since praise does not depend on circumstances.
connection: Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold its destruction (Luke 19:41-44). Hebrews 9:26 says Christ has appeared “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself,” the atonement for which this psalm cries. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness to those who confess. John 10:11-16 shows Jesus as the shepherd who gathers his sheep. 1 Peter 2:25 says we have returned to the Shepherd.
application:
Practice confession as part of lament. Name your sins and ask God to atone for them.

Ask for God’s help for the sake of his name, not just your own comfort.

Tell someone younger the story of one thing God has done for you.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help for the glory of his name.
Ask him not to remember your former iniquities.
Ask him to let his compassion come to meet you.
